name: Bill Hagerty
bio: Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Tennessee Commissioner of Economic and Community Development. Trump-endorsed; $5.3M cash on hand.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Hagerty participated in the Senate Appropriations Committee FY 2026 hearing covering Head Start and childcare funding, which maintained Head Start at FY 2025 enacted levels. His earlier support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included quadrupling the employer-provided childcare tax credit. No new Hagerty-specific public statements on early childhood education or pre-K were found in the June 14–29, 2026 window.
early_childhood_ed.details: As a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Hagerty participated in Senate Hearing 119-68 (published June 23, 2026) covering FY 2026 appropriations for Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education. The hearing addressed Head Start funding, maintained at the FY 2025 enacted level, and childcare access for working families. The administration's stated priorities for Head Start included expanding parental choice, increasing program efficiency, and promoting parental engagement through faith-based centers. Hagerty's prior legislative record includes voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which quadrupled the employer-provided childcare tax credit. No Hagerty floor statements, press releases, or public remarks specifically about early childhood education or pre-K were identified in the June 14–29, 2026 search window.

child_hunger.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which cut federal SNAP funding by an estimated $186–$300 billion over a decade. As of June 2026, approximately 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits since the law took effect. A July 2026 Tennessee SNAP junk-food restriction was temporarily blocked by a federal court in late June 2026. No new Hagerty statements on SNAP or child hunger were found in June 14–29, 2026.
child_hunger.details: The Tennessee Lookout reported on June 16, 2026 that nearly 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP food assistance since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect in July 2025 — a decline from 696,000 recipients in July 2025 to 597,890 in May 2026. The law cut $186 billion from SNAP nationally and expanded work and school requirements, removing prior exemptions for individuals over 55, veterans, and those experiencing homelessness. Separately, Tennessee had sought to restrict SNAP purchases of soda, candy, and other processed foods beginning in July 2026, but a federal judge temporarily blocked those restrictions on June 23, 2026 in response to a lawsuit by SNAP participants. A ProPublica report published June 17, 2026 found more than 770,000 children nationally are no longer receiving SNAP benefits. No new statements or actions by Hagerty specifically addressing SNAP or child hunger were identified in the June 14–29, 2026 search window.

parental_support.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which raised the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $2,200 per child, made it permanent, and indexed it to inflation. The same law quadrupled the employer-provided childcare tax credit. No new Hagerty-specific statements on paid family leave, parental financial support, or childcare costs were found in the June 14–29, 2026 window.
parental_support.details: Hagerty's primary legislative action on parental financial support remains his July 2025 vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That law permanently raised the Child Tax Credit to $2,200 per child and indexed it to inflation, and it quadrupled the employer-provided childcare tax credit. As a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Hagerty participated in FY 2026 appropriations hearings (published June 23, 2026) that addressed childcare access for working families and Head Start funding. Tennessee also saw passage of a state law in spring 2026 requiring immigration status reporting for families receiving state benefits, including the Children's Special Services program for disabled and chronically ill children, affecting approximately 400 families; Hagerty made no publicly identified statements on this state-level action during the June 14–29 window.
